node.title: VDAC channels in the outer mitochondrial membrane
node.canonical_question: What is the role of VDAC channels in the outer mitochondrial membrane?
node.summary: VDAC (voltage-dependent anion channels) are the main pores in the outer mitochondrial membrane. They allow metabolites such as ATP, ADP, and pyruvate to cross freely, while their gating state controls the overall flux of molecules in and out of the organelle.

render.heading: VDAC channels in the outer mitochondrial membrane
render.body:
The outer mitochondrial membrane is studded with protein pores called VDACs, short for voltage-dependent anion channels. Unlike the tight inner membrane, the outer membrane is relatively open to small molecules, and VDACs are the main gateway responsible for that openness.

VDACs form barrel-shaped pores built from beta-sheet strands. In their open state they allow small charged molecules to pass freely: ATP, ADP, pyruvate, NADH, and various ions can all move between the cytoplasm and the intermembrane space through these channels.

The name "voltage-dependent" comes from the fact that VDACs can change their gating state in response to the electric potential across the outer membrane. When they close or switch to a cation-selective state, the flow of anionic metabolites like ATP is reduced. This gives the cell a way to regulate how much energy currency leaves the mitochondrion.

VDACs also interact with proteins involved in apoptosis (programmed cell death), such as members of the BCL-2 family, and are thought to form part of the permeability transition pore complex. Because of this, VDAC gating is linked not only to energy metabolism but also to cell survival decisions.

In summary, VDACs are the major metabolite conduit of the outer membrane. They keep the intermembrane space in chemical communication with the cytoplasm and participate in broader cellular signalling.
